blocks.text: 1. Rate Limiting
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308230-466546123.png

Multi-Tenancy named resource limits per tenant as the safeguard against one heavy user degrading others. Rate Limiting, capping how many requests a caller can make in a given time window, is the concrete mechanism that actually enforces that safeguard.
It counts a caller's recent requests and rejects new ones once a defined limit is reached.
2. Rate Limiting Is The Direct Fix For Noisy Neighbors
Resource limits per tenant was named as the safeguard against one heavy user degrading others in Multi-Tenancy.
Rate limiting is the concrete mechanism that actually enforces that per-caller limit.

blocks.text: 3. Fixed Window Versus Sliding Window Limits

blocks.alt: Fixed Window Versus Sliding Window Limits
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308230-471861899.png
A fixed window resets its count at a set clock boundary, allowing a burst right at the reset.
A sliding window instead counts requests over a continuously moving recent time span.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Window type","Burst behavior at the boundary"],"rows":[["Fixed window","Allows a burst right when the count resets"],["Sliding window","Smooths request counting continuously over time"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Per-User Versus Per-Endpoint Limits
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441308230-564636781.png
A cheap endpoint can tolerate a much higher limit than an expensive one like full generation, echoing how Embedding Cache reduces latency and not just cost.
Rate limits can be scoped per user, per endpoint, or both together.
5. What Happens When The Limit Is Hit

blocks.alt: What Happens When The Limit Is Hit
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441448676-950380627.png
A rejected request needs a clear response telling the caller exactly why and when to retry, the same discipline as validating arguments before executing in Tool Calling.
A silent failure is far worse than an explicit rate limit response.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A rejected request that returns a clear status explaining the limit and when to retry lets a legitimate caller recover gracefully, unlike a silent failure that looks indistinguishable from a real system error.

blocks.text: 6. Rate Limiting Protects Downstream Costs, Not Just Latency

blocks.alt: Rate Limiting Protects Downstream Costs, Not Just Latency
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441448678-929761711.png
Every unthrottled request triggers real embedding and generation costs downstream, the same reasoning token cost concern raised in Chain Of Thought.
Rate limiting bounds real spend, not just response time.
7. Rate Limiting Complements Caching, Not Replaces It

blocks.alt: Rate Limiting Complements Caching, Not Replaces It
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441448679-30890716.png
Rate limiting bounds how many requests get through at all, while caching, which trades storage for repeated compute, reduces the cost of the ones that do.
The two techniques address different parts of the same cost and load problem.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Rate limiting and caching together address different halves of the same problem: rate limiting bounds how many requests arrive, while caching lowers the cost of the ones that make it through.

blocks.text: 8. Too Strict A Limit Frustrates Real Legitimate Traffic
A limit set too low blocks real, legitimate usage along with any abuse, the same friction tradeoff behind security adding friction by design in Security.
Tuning the actual limit value is as important as having a limit at all.
9. Recognizing When Rate Limiting Is Worth The Added Friction

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Rate Limiting Is Worth The Added Friction
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441448679-287855819.png
A system exposed to unpredictable or shared traffic needs rate limiting.
A fully trusted, single internal caller may not need rate limiting at all.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates a sliding window rate limiter with per-endpoint limits and a clear rejection message.

code.content:
import time

request_log = {}
LIMITS = {"search": 5, "generate": 2}
WINDOW_SECONDS = 60

def is_allowed(user_id, endpoint):
    # sliding window: only count requests within the recent window
    now = time.time()
    key = (user_id, endpoint)
    recent = [t for t in request_log.get(key, []) if now - t < WINDOW_SECONDS]
    request_log[key] = recent

    limit = LIMITS.get(endpoint, 10)
    if len(recent) >= limit:
        # reject with a clear reason and retry hint
        return False, f"Rate limit exceeded for '{endpoint}', try again in {WINDOW_SECONDS} seconds"

    recent.append(now)
    request_log[key] = recent
    return True, "Request allowed"

for i in range(3):
    allowed, message = is_allowed("user1", "generate")
    print(f"Generate request {i + 1}: {message}")

for i in range(6):
    allowed, message = is_allowed("user1", "search")
    print(f"Search request {i + 1}: {allowed}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the third generate request rejected against its lower per-endpoint limit while search requests keep succeeding up to their own higher limit, exactly the per-endpoint scoping described above.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Applying the same rate limit to a cheap endpoint and an expensive one like full generation.
Silently dropping a rate-limited request instead of returning a clear explanation and retry hint.
Treating rate limiting as a replacement for caching instead of a complementary technique.
Setting a limit so strict it blocks legitimate traffic along with any actual abuse.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Rate limiting caps how many requests a caller can make in a given time window.
It is the concrete mechanism enforcing the per-tenant resource limits named in Multi-Tenancy.
A fixed window resets at a clock boundary, allowing bursts; a sliding window smooths counting continuously.
Rate limits can be scoped per user, per endpoint, or both, matching cost to the actual endpoint.
A rejected request needs a clear response explaining why and when to retry, not a silent failure.
Rate limiting bounds real downstream compute spend, not just response latency.
Rate limiting bounds how many requests get through; caching reduces the cost of the ones that do.
A limit set too strict blocks legitimate traffic along with any actual abuse.
